title: The Worst Good Idea in Human History
subtitle: Planting seeds made us sicker, shorter, and more overworked than our ancestors. It also built literally everything. Both things are true.
hook: For ~200,000 years humans were foragers — roaming, grabbing what nature offered, working shockingly few hours. Then, about 12,000 years ago, some genius planted seeds and waited. And here's the twist historians love: for the individual human, it was arguably a *terrible* deal — worse diet, backbreaking labour, new diseases. Yet it produced cities, kings, writing, money, and you reading this. Farming is the deal humanity couldn't refuse. First lesson of the History track.

sections.heading: The one word that changed everything: surplus
sections.body:
Foragers ate what they found. Farmers *produced* food — and, crucially, produced **more than they needed right now**. That leftover is the hinge of all history: **surplus**.

Surplus meant not everyone had to chase dinner. Suddenly some people could do something *else* full-time — make pots, forge weapons, pray, rule, keep records. That's **specialization**, and it's the engine behind every complex society that followed. No surplus, no specialists, no civilization.

sections.caption: The chain reaction the rest of this track is built on: farming → surplus → specialists → cities → states, taxes, writing.

sections.label: The catch nobody mentions
sections.body: Early farmers were often *worse off* than foragers: longer hours, a dull grain-heavy diet, shorter stature, and shiny new diseases from crowding together with animals. Stored surplus could also be **stolen** — hello taxes, warfare, and the first real inequality. Farming won not because it made people *happier*, but because it made *more* people and more power. Quantity beat quality.

sections.label: It happened 7+ times, alone
sections.body: Farming was invented **independently** — Fertile Crescent, China, Mesoamerica, the Andes, and more — by peoples who never met. When that many separate groups stumble on the same trick, it's a clue that the *conditions* (a stable, warming climate after the Ice Age) were ripe. History is driven by circumstance, not just heroes.

sections.caption: Crash Course's legendary opener on the Agricultural Revolution and its brutal trade-offs.

takeaways: ~12,000 years ago humans went from **foraging to farming** — producing food, not just finding it.
The real product was **surplus**: more food than needed right now.
Surplus freed people to **specialize** → cities → states, taxes, writing.
For individuals it was often a *downgrade* (disease, toil, inequality) — but it made more people and power.
Invented **independently** in many places → conditions, not lone geniuses, drive history.

quiz.q: What was farming's real game-changing output?
quiz.explain: Surplus — extra food beyond immediate need — is what freed people to specialize.

quiz.q: Why do historians call it a mixed blessing?
options: Early farmers often worked harder, ate worse, and got new diseases
quiz.explain: The individual deal was rough; the species-level payoff (more people, more power) is why it stuck.

quiz.q: BOSS: Farming appeared independently on multiple continents around the same era. Best takeaway?
options: One civilization secretly taught the rest
Shared conditions (post-Ice-Age climate) made it ripe everywhere — circumstance drives history
It was random luck each time
quiz.explain: Independent invention screams 'the conditions were right', a theme you'll see repeat across this whole track.

tg_quiz.correct: Yes — surplus is what built civilization.
tg_quiz.wrong: It's surplus — the leftover food that freed people to specialize.
tg_quiz.explain: No surplus, no specialists, no cities.
